crops.wild: Wild einkorn (Triticum monococcum subsp. aegilopoides, syn. T. boeoticum)
crops.wild_look: Short grass under 70 cm, not very productive; ripe ears shatter and drop their kernels, which sit in tough husks (glumes).
crops.changes: Ear stays intact when ripe (non-shattering), so it can be reaped; slightly larger kernels. Self-pollination helped keep the new traits.

spread.note: Einkorn introduced to Cyprus c. 7500 BC
Wheats reach Britain and Scandinavia by 4000 BC
Declines in favour of emmer from c. 2000 BCE

crops.today: A niche hulled wheat; contains gluten and more protein than modern red wheats.
crops.fact: Models once claimed domestication could take 20–200 years; archaeology shows over a thousand years of pre-domestication cultivation.

img.artist: Albert Meyer (illustrator of Leonhart Fuchs's herbal, 1543)
img.shows: Einkorn plant, woodcut from Fuchs 1543 (domesticated)
Wild einkorn (T. boeoticum) growing on Karadağ, Karaman province, Turkey

crops.cult_note: Wild einkorn gathered at Abu Hureyra (c. 10,700–9000 BC) and Mureybet (c. 9800–9300 BC); wheat cultivation in the Fertile Crescent from c. 9600 BC
crops.dom_note: Domestic form after c. 8800 BC at Çayönü, Cafer Höyük and possibly Nevalı Çori; genetics also suggest several domestications

crops.wild: Wild emmer (Triticum turgidum subsp. dicoccoides), itself a hybrid of wild Triticum urartu × goatgrass Aegilops speltoides
crops.wild_look: Grass 50–70 cm with 10–15 cm awned ears that shatter when ripe; spikelets drill into the soil with their awns; chaff hard to remove.
crops.changes: Ears no longer shatter, so whole spikelets can be harvested (hulled emmer); later free-threshing forms whose grains fall free when threshed.
crops.centre: Çayönü, SE Anatolia (genetics: domesticated once in SE Anatolia)

spread.note: Introduced to Cyprus as early as 8600 BC
Small amounts in Period 1, 7000–5000 BC
Emmer reaches Greece by 6500 BC
Shortly after 6000 BC; later main Pharaonic wheat
Reaches Germany and Spain by 5000 BC

crops.today: Still grown; one of the three grains sold as farro in Italy.
crops.fact: Emmer was the main wheat of Pharaonic Egypt; with barley it was the basis of Egyptian bread and beer.

img.shows: Black emmer in a field near Allmendingen, Germany (colour photo)
Wild emmer growing in spring in Israel

crops.cult_note: Wild emmer first cultivated in the southern Levant as early as 9600 BC; wild grains at Netiv HaGdud (PPNA)
crops.dom_note: Çayönü c. 8300–7600 BC: spikelet scars of a hulled domestic type; Tell Aswad c. 8500–8200 BC claimed (less reliable grain-size method); location still debated

crops.wild: No wild ancestor: hybrid of a domesticated tetraploid (emmer-type) wheat × Tausch's goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii)
crops.wild_look: The goatgrass parent is a wild annual grass of the Caucasus, Caspian and Central Asia; it gave wheat its D genome.
crops.changes: Six chromosome sets (four from emmer, two from goatgrass), free-threshing grain; 20th-century dwarfing genes (Norin 10) powered the Green Revolution.

spread.note: Oldest hexaploid wheat (DNA), 6400–6200 BC
Wheat cultivated in India around 3500 BC
Wheat likely appears around 2600 BC
Juan Garrido sows first wheat in New Spain, 1520s
Prairie colonisation makes North America a grain exporter

crops.today: ~95% of all wheat; wheat (799 Mt, 2024) covers more land than any food crop.
crops.fact: World trade in wheat is greater than that of all other crops combined.

img.shows: Colour plate of a flowering wheat plant and ripe ear
Spike of the wild goatgrass parent Aegilops tauschii (small, 196 px)

crops.cult_note: Arose spontaneously in farmers' fields of already-domesticated wheat
crops.dom_note: Originated c. 8,000 years ago; oldest hexaploid wheat DNA from Çatalhöyük seeds, c. 6400–6200 BC

crops.wild: Wild barley (Hordeum vulgare subsp. spontaneum)
crops.wild_look: Two-rowed ear with hulled grains and a brittle spike that falls apart when ripe; ground into flour at Ohalo II 23,000 years ago.
crops.changes: Non-brittle ear (Bt1/Bt2 mutations), then naked (hulless) and six-rowed forms with three fertile spikelets per node; grains became rounder.
crops.centre: Tell Aswad, Syria (earliest domestic two-row barley)

spread.note: First six-rowed barley, 9350–8950 years ago
Domesticated barley reaches eastern Finland by 4200 BC
Harappan barley, 5,700–3,300 years ago
Grown since Early Mumun period, c. 1500–850 BC
Staple of Tibetan cuisine since the 5th century AD

crops.today: Fourth grain by quantity (146 Mt, 2023); 70% feeds animals, 30% beer, whisky, food.
crops.fact: Barley beer was probably one of the first alcoholic drinks; barley later served as currency (Sumerian ration tablets).

crops.cult_note: Gilgal I granary of thousands of wild barley grains, c. 11,700–10,550 years ago: cultivation before domestication
crops.dom_note: Domestic two-row barley at Tell Aswad, c. 10,200–9,550 years ago; Jarmo 9000–7000 BC; Tibet and Ethiopia possibly extra centres (debated)

crops.wild: Wild lentil (Lens culinaris subsp. orientalis / Lens orientalis)
crops.wild_look: Small bushy herb; wild pods burst open to scatter seeds, and the seeds stay dormant instead of sprouting together.
crops.changes: Pods that stay closed (indehiscent), seeds without dormancy, and seed size rising through the PPNB (Yiftah'el seeds ~4.2 mm wide).

spread.note: Carbonised lentils, 6250–5950 BC
Lentils 6000–5000 BC
Lentils 5500–5000 BC
Lentils appear c. 2500–2000 BC

crops.today: 7 Mt dry lentils (2023), 72% from Australia, Canada and India.
crops.fact: At Yiftah'el, Israel, archaeologists found a hoard of more than one million carbonised lentils about 10,000 years old.

crops.cult_note: Pre-domestication cultivation at Jerf el Ahmar (Syria) and Netiv HaGdud, c. 11,000 cal BP (PPNA); wild lentils gathered at Ohalo II 23,000 BP
crops.dom_note: Yiftah'el hoard of >1 million lentils, 10,100–9,700 cal BP: widely cultivated; full domestication during the PPNB (one review dates Yiftah'el 6800 BC)

crops.wild: Wild pea (Pisum sativum subsp. elatius); P. fulvum gave a second, separate domestication
crops.wild_look: Climbing wild vine of the Mediterranean and Near East; ripe pods split open to shed seeds, which have rough coats and stay dormant.
crops.changes: Pods that stay shut, seeds that sprout without dormancy, smoother seed coats and bigger seeds; genomics shows two independent domestications.

spread.note: Early finds c. 4800–4400 BC
Present in the 5th millennium BC
Pea finds date back to 4000 BC
Harappan peas 2250–1750 BC

crops.today: 21.5 Mt green peas (2023); China and India grow 86%.
crops.fact: Gregor Mendel's mid-19th-century pea crosses founded genetics, but were ignored until about 1900.

crops.dom_note: Smooth-coated domestic peas 5850–5600 BC; Wikipedia: seeds with domestic traits ≥7,000 years old in Turkey (slow change)

crops.wild: Cicer reticulatum (closest wild relative, interfertile)
crops.wild_look: Rare wild annual of a small area of SE Turkey and nearby Syria; smaller seeds that need a dormancy period and ripen unevenly.
crops.changes: Large palatable seeds without dormancy, seeds easy to free from pods, even ripening, and a shift to spring sowing.

spread.note: Chickpeas dated 5450 BCE
Several sites, 1750–1500 BCE
Bronze Age chickpeas, 1400 BCE
Spanish and Portuguese bring chickpeas, 16th century

crops.today: India grows 75% of the world's chickpeas (2023).
crops.fact: Genomes of 3,366 chickpeas show a strong bottleneck about 10,000 years ago, the mark of domestication.

crops.wild: Pale flax (Linum bienne)
crops.wild_look: Slender pale-blue flax from Western Europe to the Caucasus; its wild fibres were spun and dyed 30,000 years ago (Dzudzuana Cave).
crops.changes: First selected for oil: bigger seeds (Tell Ramad); later tall fibre types for linen. Early domesticates still had seed capsules that split open.

spread.note: Flax reaches Switzerland and Germany by 5,000 years ago
Cultivated at least 5,000 years ago
Charlemagne revives flax growing, 8th century

crops.today: 876,000 t fibre flax (2022), 75% grown in France.
crops.fact: Ancient Egyptian priests wore only linen, and mummies were wrapped in it.

crops.cult_note: First appears at Tell es-Sultan (Jericho), c. 9900–9550 years ago
crops.dom_note: Domestic oilseed flax with larger seeds at Tell Ramad, and flax fabric at Çatalhöyük, by c. 9,000 years ago

crops.wild: Wild olive / oleaster (Olea europaea var. sylvestris)
crops.wild_look: Wild olive trees have smaller, thinner-fleshed fruits than cultivated trees.
crops.changes: Bigger, fleshier, oil-rich fruit; good trees cloned by cuttings, layering or grafting, because trees from seed yield poorly.

spread.place: Submerged settlement south of Haifa (Kfar Samir)
spread.note: Olive oil production c. 4500 BC
Earliest olive oil amphorae, Early Minoan, 3500 BC
Palace archives record royal olive lands, 2400 BC
Olives reach the Americas, 16th century (sources differ)

crops.today: Spain makes about 25% of world olive oil; the EU nearly 60%.
crops.fact: About 100,000 years ago people on Morocco's Atlantic coast used olive wood for fuel and probably ate olives.

crops.wild: Wild grapevine (Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris)
crops.wild_look: Forest climber with male and female flowers on separate plants; only pollinated females bear small (~6 mm) dark berries.
crops.changes: Hermaphrodite self-pollinating flowers; much bigger berries (up to 3 cm), green, red or black; narrower pips.

spread.note: Wine residues in jars, c. 5000 BC
Wine production by c. 4500 BC
Oldest known winery, c. 4100 BC
Vineyards established in Mexico by 1530
Vineyards in Peru by the 1550s, Chile soon after

crops.today: Vitis vinifera grapes make the majority of the world's wine.
crops.fact: Armenia's Areni-1 cave held a 6,000-year-old winery: wine press, fermentation vats, jars and cups.

crops.wild: Uncertain: wild/feral Phoenix dactylifera; North African dates also share genome with Cretan Phoenix theophrasti
crops.wild_look: Tall palm with separate male and female trees; only females bear fruit, and only when wind carries pollen from a male.
crops.changes: Hand-pollination, so one male can serve up to 100 females; growers keep mostly fruiting females and select sweet varieties.

crops.wild: Wild fig / caprifig (wild Ficus carica)
crops.wild_look: Wild figs depend on the tiny fig wasp Blastophaga psenes; without pollination the fruit tends to drop.
crops.changes: A seedless parthenocarpic mutant that ripens without wasps; kept alive only by planting cut branches (vegetative propagation).
crops.centre: Gilgal I, Jordan Valley (13 km north of Jericho)

De Agri Cultura lists five fig strains
Junípero Serra's missionaries bring first figs

crops.today: 1.26 Mt figs (2020); Turkey grows a quarter.
crops.fact: Gilgal's figs may be the oldest known crop, about a thousand years before wheat and barley (debated).

crops.wild: Wild Sorghum bicolor (wild races; usually named subsp. verticilliflorum — not stated in Wikipedia)
crops.wild_look: Tall wild savanna grass of north-east Africa; ripe grains drop from the head (shattering).
crops.changes: Non-shattering heads holding up to 3,000 seeds; first race (bicolor) kept tight husks; later races caudatum, durra and guinea suited new regions.

spread.note: Sorghum bread in graves, c. 3100 BCE
Reaches India around 4,000 years ago
Reaches West Africa about 3,000 years ago
Spread by the Arab Agricultural Revolution, Middle Ages

crops.today: World's fifth most important cereal; 57 Mt (2023), US grows 14%.
crops.fact: A piece of sorghum bread from a Predynastic Egyptian grave, about 5,100 years old, is in Turin's Egyptian Museum.

crops.wild: Wild pearl millet (Pennisetum violaceum, classed within P. glaucum since 1977)
crops.wild_look: Bristly wild grass of the southern Sahara and Sahel with small grains that fall when ripe (shattering).
crops.changes: Non-shattering heads, larger grains and stalked spikelet clusters; extremely hardy—grows where drought, poor soil and heat defeat maize or wheat.

Arrives 2000–1700 BC (other sources 1500–1100 BCE)

crops.today: Most widely grown millet; India is the largest producer.
crops.fact: In Nigeria it is grown mixed with sorghum and cowpea, so one crop's failure never ruins the whole harvest.

crops.dom_note: Domesticated pearl millet impressed in pottery, Tilemsi Valley, Mali, 2500–2000 BCE (Manning et al. 2011)

crops.wild: Wild African rice (Oryza barthii)
crops.wild_look: Wild rice of open West African wetlands; its seed heads shatter, scattering the grains as they ripen.
crops.changes: Less shattering (though on average about half the grains still fall); hardy: tolerates deep water, drought, iron toxicity and poor soils.

crops.fact: Enslaved West African rice farmers brought both the seed and the know-how; planters marketed captives for their rice skills.

crops.wild: Wild Coffea arabica of Ethiopian forests (itself a natural hybrid of C. canephora × C. eugenioides)
crops.wild_look: Forest tree 9–12 m tall with open branches, wild in south Ethiopia, South Sudan's Boma Plateau and Yemen.
crops.changes: Grown as pruned shrubs on terraced Yemeni slopes; nearly all arabica varieties descend from plants farmed in Yemen.

First mainland European coffeehouse, 1645
Arabica production begins in Indonesia, 1699
Gabriel de Clieu brings seedlings to the New World
Becomes world's largest coffee producer by 1852

crops.fact: Arabica was born as a natural hybrid of two coffee species between 1.08 million and 543,000 years ago.

crops.wild: Dioscorea praehensilis (forest yam), possibly with D. abyssinica (savanna) by hybridisation

crops.wild: Common wild rice (Oryza rufipogon)
crops.wild_look: Marsh grass whose awned grains drop (shatter) as they ripen, so most seed fell before anyone could harvest it.

Dapenkeng culture farmers

crops.changes: Selected for thick, juicy, sweet stems, propagated from stem cuttings; hybrids with wild S. spontaneum gave the hardy canes of Asia.

crops.wild: Not a wild species: hybrid of pomelo (Citrus maxima) and mandarin (Citrus reticulata)
crops.wild_look: No wild sweet orange exists. Its ancestors, wild pomelo and mandarin, descend from small berries; some mandarins are too sour to eat.
crops.changes: One ancient cross, about 42% pomelo and 58% mandarin; every sweet orange is a clone of it, differing only by selected bud mutations (e.g. navel).

crops.wild: Exact wild ancestor unknown (Old World A-genome cottons)
crops.wild_look: Shrub 1-2 m tall with maple-like leaves; seeds sit in capsules (bolls) covered in fibre hairs.

crops.today: Upland cotton from Mexico gives 90% of world output; India is the largest producer.
crops.fact: Megasthenes told Seleucus I of Indian 'trees on which wool grows' - probably tree cotton.

crops.wild: Balsas teosinte (Zea mays subsp. parviglumis)
crops.wild_look: Short, bushy grass; each tiny 'ear' holds 5-10 seeds, each sealed in a very hard fruitcase, and the ear breaks apart when ripe.

before_farming.t: Fisher-hunter-gatherer camp c. 23,000 years ago: 90,000+ seeds of 100+ species; wild barley and grasses ground on a stone slab; sickle wear on flints.
Natufian hearths, 14,400 years ago: charred flatbread-like remains of wild einkorn, barley or oat flour mixed with ~50,000 club-rush tubers—4,000 years before farming.
Natufian foragers (c. 12,500–9500 BCE) gathered wild cereals, legumes, almonds, acorns and pistachios, and hunted mountain gazelle.
Foragers harvested 'wild gardens' of einkorn, emmer and rye and hunted gazelle; rye cultivation claimed from 11,050 BCE in the Younger Dryas (debated).
From c. 9500 BCE: over 7,000 grinding stones show heavy cereal processing (wild or cultivated unclear); gazelle hunted midsummer to autumn amid wild einkorn and barley.
World's oldest pottery, c. 14,500 BCE. Jōmon foragers ate chestnuts, beechnuts, acorns (tannins processed out), salmon, shellfish, sika deer and wild boar.
Camp eating seaweed (nine species, from a coast 60 km away, dated 14,220–13,980 years ago), tubers, seeds, nuts, berries and wild potato. Dating debated.
Clovis points found with Pleistocene animal bones (c. 11,500 BCE); whether Clovis people were big-game specialists or mixed foragers is disputed.
Independent farming: wetland drained by ditches about 9,000 years ago to grow taro; deliberate banana planting 6,950–6,550 years ago. UNESCO site.
